name: Nursery glider and rocking recliner
tagline: A heavy chair in two or three pieces, with a glide mechanism underneath and a pinch point you need to know about.
peopleNote: Two people. Gliders are genuinely heavy and the back has to be held upright while it locks on.

tools.why: Most gliders are back-slides-onto-frame with no tools at all.
Some models bolt the back on, and most ottomans bolt together.
Opening the packaging. Cut away from the upholstery with a short blade.

provided: Bolts and Allen key on some models
before: Unwrap it in the nursery. A glider rarely fits through a doorway assembled, and the packaging protects it on the way in.
Clear a space bigger than the chair. A glider needs clearance behind it to glide, and a reclining one needs considerably more.
Check which way up the back goes before you lift it. It is heavy and you do not want to find out mid-lift.
safety: The glide mechanism underneath is a pinch point. Small fingers and toes fit into it and it closes with your full body weight behind it. Keep children and pets clear while it is moving.
Never let a child play on or under a glider, and never let one glide while a toddler is on the floor beside it.
Recliners have a second pinch point in the footrest mechanism. Keep it closed when not in use.
Do not lift a glider by its arms or its back. Lift the frame.

steps.title: Unwrap in the room, cutting away from the fabric
steps.say: Bring it in wrapped and cut the plastic in the room where it lands. Short blade, angled away from the upholstery.
do: Carry it in still wrapped
Cut along a seam of the plastic
Bag the plastic straight away
steps.watch: More new upholstered furniture is damaged by the unwrapping knife than by the delivery.

steps.title: Set the base down and check it glides
steps.say: Put the seat base in place and push it back and forth. It should glide smoothly and silently before you add anything else.
do: Base on the floor where the chair will live
Push it through its full travel
Listen for grinding or knocking
steps.tip: Test it now, while the chair is light and you can still turn it over to look underneath.
steps.watch: Shipping bolts or a transit lock are fitted on some models and must come off before use. Check underneath for a bracket or zip tie that does not belong.

steps.title: Find the back's locking channels
steps.say: Most glider backs slide down into two steel channels on the frame. Look at the bottom of the back section — you will see two hooks or tongues.
do: Turn the back and find the hooks on its lower edge
Find the matching channels on the chair frame
Check for any levers that have to be flipped open first
steps.tip: Some models have small locking levers inside the channels that must be flipped up before the back goes in and down afterwards. Easy to miss, and the back will not stay on without them.

steps.title: Slide the back on — two people
steps.say: One person each side, line the hooks up with the channels, and push the back straight down until it drops and seats with a solid thunk.
do: Both sides lined up before pushing
Push straight down, firmly and evenly
Keep pushing until it stops moving
steps.watch: If one side goes in and the other does not, lift it out and start again. Forcing one side in at an angle bends the channel and that damage is permanent.

steps.title: Lock the back and lift-test it
steps.say: Flip down any locking levers, then grab the top of the back and pull upward hard. It must not lift off.
do: Locking levers down, both sides
Pull up firmly on the top of the back
Push the back from behind too
steps.tip: Do this before anyone sits in it. A back that is seated but not locked feels completely normal until someone leans back hard.
steps.watch: This is the step that catches people out. The chair looks finished and works fine, and then the back comes off months later.

steps.title: Build the ottoman
steps.say: The ottoman usually has four legs that bolt on, and sometimes its own glide mechanism. Start every bolt by hand, then tighten.
do: Ottoman upside down on a soft surface
All bolts started by hand first
Tighten in a diagonal pattern, then a second lap
steps.tip: If the ottoman glides too, check it is not fitted with a transit lock either.

steps.title: Understand the pinch point
steps.say: Look underneath while someone glides it slowly. You will see the scissor linkage open and close. That gap closes with the full weight of an adult behind it.
do: Have someone glide it slowly while you look underneath
Note where the linkage closes
Show anyone else in the house, especially older children
steps.watch: Crushed fingers and toes from glider mechanisms are a well-known nursery injury. The danger is highest when a toddler is on the floor beside a chair being used at night in the dark.

steps.title: Set the recline and the lock, if it has one
steps.say: Test the recline through its full range and find the glide lock. Most gliders have one, and locking it when you stand up is a good habit.
do: Recline fully and return
Find the glide lock lever, usually underneath or on the side
Check the footrest closes fully and stays closed
steps.tip: Lock the glide when you get out of the chair with a baby in your arms. It stops the chair moving as you stand.

steps.title: Sit, glide, and check for noise
steps.say: Sit properly and glide for a minute. Any knock, squeak or catch is worth chasing now rather than at three in the morning.
do: Full weight, full travel, both directions
Listen for knocking from the mechanism
Check the back for any movement relative to the seat
steps.tip: A glider that squeaks when new usually just needs the mechanism pivots lubricated — a drop of light machine oil, not a spray.

steps.title: Position it and set a reminder
steps.say: Leave clearance behind and beside it. Then set a reminder, because glider bolts loosen under cyclic loading faster than almost any other furniture.
do: Clearance behind for the full glide and recline
Not against a wall or a radiator
Three-monthly reminder to re-tighten and re-test the back lock
steps.watch: A glider is used thousands of times, in the dark, by a tired person holding a baby. It earns its checks.

recheck.what: Pull up hard on the top of the back. It must not lift. Back-locking levers are the thing that quietly works loose.
Re-tighten every bolt on the chair and the ottoman. Gliding is cyclic loading and it loosens fasteners steadily.
Look underneath at the glide mechanism for wear, loose pivots or missing fasteners.
A squeak is a dry or loose pivot. Tighten first, then lubricate with a drop of light machine oil.
Re-brief everyone in the house on the pinch point underneath, and consider locking the glide when the chair is not in use.

fixes.q: The back will not slide into the frame
fixes.a: Check for locking levers inside the channels that need flipping open first, and make sure you have the back the right way round. Line both sides up and push straight down with even pressure — going in at an angle will jam it.

fixes.q: The back lifts off when I lean forward
fixes.a: The locking levers are not engaged. Find them inside or beside the channels and flip them down. Then pull up hard to confirm.

fixes.q: It will not glide, or glides stiffly
fixes.a: Look underneath for a transit lock or shipping bracket that was never removed. If it is clear, check the mechanism bolts are not overtightened — a crushed pivot binds.
Tighten every bolt in the mechanism first. If it persists, a drop of light machine oil on each pivot usually silences it. Avoid spray lubricants near upholstery.

fixes.q: The chair rocks unevenly on my floor
fixes.a: Check for felt pads or leveling feet on the base. Gliders are sensitive to uneven floors because the whole mechanism is referenced off the base.

fixes.q: My toddler put their fingers in the mechanism
fixes.a: That is the known hazard with this product. Lock the glide when the chair is not in use, and keep the area beside the chair clear when a toddler is mobile.
